transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08 UTC
Start: 16:00 Z
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Patel (AE), Liam O'Connor (SE) - Redwood; Caroline Nguyen, Dev Patel, Samir Rao, Elena Torres - LedgerFlow
Recording quality: medium (occasional word swaps)

--- Automated summary (short):
Redwood demo of long-context + high TPS streaming failure modes, showed cache strategies, fallback model routing, and backpressure handling. LedgerFlow asks for benchmark, pricing, and VPC networking notes.

00:00:05 Maya: Alright, hi everyone, thanks for taking time. Quick roll call, uh, I'm Maya, I'm the account lead, and Liam's our systems engineer who'll drive the demo.
00:00:18 Liam: Hey all, thanks, I'll share my screen in a sec. We're going to reproduce three patterns you called out: long context sessions, sustained TPS bursts, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. We'll push realistic traces you sent, Dev, and show mitigation knobs.
00:00:36 Caroline: Perfect. Our big worry is—sorry—if the streaming client gets a 504 mid-response because some gateway times out, what do users see and how do we recover?
00:00:49 Liam: Great question. So by default, if a client-side transport timeout happens, the token stream stops; however, on the server side we keep the KV cache and the partial context so a reconnect can resume from the last cache checkpoint if you reattach with the same session id. There is a caveat—
00:01:10 Dev: Sorry Liam, when you say resume, it's not magically reconstructing in-flight tokens, right? We need idempotency keys or something?
00:01:20 Liam: Correct, we expose an idempotency/session ID header. If the client re-posts a resume request within our TTL window, we can continue generation with minimal re-computation. If the TTL expired, we fall back to a prefix-only rewarm which may incur extra cost and latency.
00:01:37 Samir: What is the TTL by default?
00:01:40 Liam: Default is 3 minutes for in-flight resume checkpoints, and 24 hours for KV cache entries for prefix warm. Those numbers are configurable—Dedicated customers can bump cache TTLs or pin certain user buckets.
00:01:54 Elena: That 24-hour window, is it per-user or per-prefix?
00:01:58 Liam: It's per-prefix key; we shard by model+tenant+prefix-hash. So similar prompts across users can share warm cache if the prefix hash matches.
00:02:11 Caroline: Okay uh, next—how do we handle backpressure? If LedgerFlow has bursts of 5k TPS for 2 minutes, we don't want huge 99.9 p99 spikes.
00:02:23 Liam: Right. We demo two things: adaptive request shedding and elastic burst lanes. For hosted mode we can do a soft-shed where we divert some requests to a cheaper smaller model variant or return a light-weight response with a rerank id. For Dedicated you have reserved burst capacity and better isolation, but costs more.
00:02:42 Dev: Can you show the stream behavior when the process hits kernel-level queue limits—like socket buffer fill?
00:02:49 Liam: Yep. I'll open the harness — we'll start a 10-minute run with a trace that matches your traffic. Note: inference runtime uses continuous batching, so you'll see throughput increase then latency step-up when queue depth passes the continuous-batching threshold.
00:03:05 [screen share starts — load generator kicking off]
00:03:15 Liam: Alright, generator ramping now. You're seeing requests per second on the top-left. We're at 1k TPS and heading up. Notice the blue line is end-to-end p95, red is p99.
00:03:33 Caroline: I see p99 creeping at 1k, that's fine, but what's the mitigation when we hit 4k?
00:03:39 Liam: Around 4k TPS you'll see our adaptive batching step in: we tighten batch time windows to prioritize latency, but that reduces GPU efficiency. Alternatively, we start model variant routing—shift low-priority traffic to the quantized variant.
00:03:55 [00:04:00] (background noise; some words unclear)
00:04:15 Dev: If rerouting happens, how do we track the provenance of the response? We need deterministic trace to audit model outputs—especially for compliance.
00:04:26 Liam: We attach route metadata to each response header (model_variant, quant_level, routing_reason), and we log the prompt hash and the chosen fallback. You can pull those from the Console or the audit logs API. There's a small caveat where streaming partial responses may be truncated if gateway timeouts occur — you'll see an error code and a resume token if available.
00:04:50 Samir: Can we force immediate failover to a replica instead of fallback to smaller model? We prefer same-model semantics.
00:04:59 Liam: We do fast replica failover for transient GPU node failures, yes. But when capacity is globally constrained, fallback to smaller-quantized variants is more cost-effective and avoids queue starvation. We can make the policy strict for you — policy rules are in the rollout config.
00:05:12 Maya: Quick interjection — LedgerFlow asked about connection pooling at the ingress. We recommend fronting with a connection proxy that supports HTTP/2 multiplexing; that reduces socket churn and helps with backpressure.
00:05:24 Caroline: Are there recommended timeout settings for APIGW/nginx? We run a 30s idle timeout currently and worried that's too small for long streaming generations.
00:05:33 Liam: For streaming you want longer idle timeouts — 120s+ recommended for long-tail streams, and allow for keepalive pings. Alternatively use the resume token pattern so clients can reconnect quickly. We'll share our nginx tuning doc.
00:05:46 Elena: Can you demo a client timeout mid-stream and then a resume?
00:05:50 Liam: Yep — switching to the 'timeout/resume' scenario.
00:05:56 [load generator simulates a network hiccup; one streaming client hits a 504]
00:06:10 Liam: You can see the stream closed on the client side; server logs show session checkpoint saved to KV store with checkpoint_id abc123. If the client sends resume with checkpoint_id within 3 minutes, we attach the cached KV and continue.
00:06:26 Dev: Does reconnect cost extra tokens? Like, do we re-send the whole prompt?
00:06:31 Liam: If within checkpoint TTL we resume with minimal re-computation. If expired, yes you'll pay to rewarm prefix cache since we need to rerun earlier layers to rebuild KV. We can also persist warmed embeddings for hot prefixes to lower that cost for Dedicated customers.
00:06:45 Caroline: How does quantization affect hallucination rate? If we fallback to an 8-bit quantized variant under load does answer quality degrade?
00:06:55 Liam: There's a measurable difference—our Optimize tool reports mean ROUGE/QA deltas for quantized variants. In practice for retrieval-augmented prompts the impact is small, but for complex reasoning there's higher variance. We'll attach a quality delta table from our internal evals.
00:07:12 Samir: Can the fallback be per-route? We have some flows where we will never accept quantized outputs.
00:07:17 Liam: Absolutely — route-level policies can mark flows as 'no-fallback', and those flows will be prioritized or shed with an error rather than routed to quantized models.
00:07:27 [00:07:30] Speaker overlap (someone coughing)
00:07:45 Liam: Now I'm going to enable aggressive burst to force queue pressure. Watch the streaming connection status on the right panel.
00:07:56 [generator ramps to 6k TPS]
00:08:07 Caroline: Whoa, p99 just spiked to 2.1s — what's the client-facing symptom? Do we drop chunks?
00:08:12 Liam: If socket buffers are full you may observe chunk delays; our runtime flushes tokens as soon as they are ready, but network-layer queuing can reorder or drop TCP segments in extreme cases — which is why we recommend HTTP/2 or WebSocket with reconnect/resume semantics.
00:08:29 Dev: Can we throttle per-user? We have heavy power users that cause noisy neighbor.
00:08:35 Liam: Yes, per-tenant and per-user rate limits are available; plus we expose per-route quotas and dynamic throttles via Redwood Console. You can configure soft quotas that return a 429 with a retry-after and hard quotas that block.
00:08:45 Elena: Regarding observability—do you provide token-level cost breakdown for each streamed response?
00:08:51 Liam: Yes, Console shows token distribution (prompt vs completion), KV cache hits, and a per-request cost estimate. For streaming we attach incremental cost metadata per flush so you can approximate mid-stream cost.
00:09:06 Caroline: About private deployments—if we go VPC does Redwood still run the Control Plane or do we self-host it?
00:09:13 Maya: For VPC you can choose either: managed control plane with private connectivity, or a customer-run control plane for air-gapped installs. Both support the same rollout and audit features, but the latter has additional compliance paperwork.
00:09:27 Samir: Ok demo looks good. Could you show logs when the gateway applied a 504? I want to see the mapping to resume token.
00:09:34 Liam: Sure — filtering logs now. See trace id tf-778; it shows event sequence: request-received -> partial-stream-flush -> client-timeout -> checkpoint-saved(abc123) -> client-disconnect.
00:09:50 Dev: That event sequence is good. Will you also show how logs look integrated into our SIEM (Splunk)?
00:09:56 Liam: We have a Splunk ingestion guide. Logs emit JSON with fields model_version, checkpoint_id, prompt_hash, routing_policy. We can stream those to your Splunk endpoint or S3.
00:10:08 [demo continues with latency/throughput graphs — approx 12 minutes of measurable load scenarios; snippets omitted for brevity]
00:22:30 Liam: Jumping to the long-context test now — we want to show context beyond typical 16k: we loaded a 200k token session partitioned across multiple segments and used prefix stitching with KV cache.
00:22:45 Caroline: 200k? That's our real user scenario — legal files stitched over months. How is memory kept efficient?
00:22:53 Liam: We shard the key-value cache across hosts and only keep the top-N most recent KV blocks in hot memory. For tails we spill to Redis/SSD depending on deployment profile. On Dedicated you can provision more hot memory or pin hot prefixes to a GPU group.
00:23:10 Dev: How does compaction work? We can't keep every token's KV forever.
00:23:15 Liam: We do LRU compaction and semantic compaction: we can compress old segments into embeddings and keep only a summarized prefix for retrieval rather than the full KV. That reduces memory while keeping relevance.
00:23:29 Samir: If we compact aggressively will retrieval-relevance degrade?
00:23:34 Liam: Minor but measurable; Optimize can simulate compaction levels vs QA deltas so you can pick an operating point.
00:23:45 Maya: Quick note — LedgerFlow had a security requirement about audit logs and KMS key rotation. We will route those questions to our security team after this demo.
00:23:56 Caroline: Anything else we should watch for in the console during the long-context run?
00:24:02 Liam: Look at the cache hit heatmap and the model-variant routing table. You'll see which user buckets are getting quantized. Also the session gap metric — that tells you if your clients are reattaching often.
00:24:16 [00:24:20] (minor transcription glitch here: 'K V cash' spelled odd)
00:24:42 Liam: We're hitting sustained 3k TPS with long-context—notice cost per 1k tokens in the lower panel. If we enable prefix compression you can see cost drop while p99 increases slightly.
00:25:00 Elena: If we want strict determinism, is there a configuration to disable compression/fallbacks entirely?
00:25:07 Liam: Yes, strict-determinism mode disables model variant fallback and any compression that changes tokenization semantics. It's viable but increases cost; usually used for regulated flows.
00:25:20 Dev: For the POC what diagnostics would you need from us?
00:25:25 Maya: We'll need sample traces (anonymized), expected API traffic shape, a list of protected routes, SSO/SAML contact for security, and a primary network contact for VPC peering.
00:25:38 Caroline: We'll send those.
00:25:42 [long pause as files are uploaded for the demo stage]
00:26:10 Liam: Now final scenario—simulated intermittent upstream network flaps to observe resume and garbage collection.
00:26:20 [flap] 00:26:40 Liam: We triggered multiple short disconnects; observe session gap spikes, but KV survived across three flaps within checkpoint TTL.
00:26:54 Dev: Good. Can the client-side library attempt transparent reconnect with backoff?
00:26:59 Liam: Yes our SDK supports exponential backoff plus resume token semantics. We'll provide the SDK with built-in reconnect behavior.
00:27:10 Caroline: On the fallback metrics—can we get an alert when more than X% of traffic is being quantized?
00:27:17 Liam: Console alerting supports that. We'll set up alerts by model_variant share and p99 latency thresholds.
00:27:25 Maya: Quick recap before we close: Redwood will send benchmark harness and plan, security docs, Dedicated pricing sheet, and a suggested POC timeline. LedgerFlow to provide traces and network contacts.
00:27:38 Samir: Sounds good. Any blockers on the Redwood side?
00:27:42 Maya: No blockers; scheduling the POC kick-off is next.
00:27:47 Caroline: Thanks everyone.
00:28:00 [call continues into Q&A and small clarifications for another 24 minutes — topics include SSO/SAML integration, audit log retention, and SLA for Dedicated. Below are selected excerpts from that section.]

00:31:10 Dev: On SSO—can we integrate with our Okta instance and map roles to per-route permissions?
00:31:18 Maya: Yes, SAML/Okta supported; role mapping via SCIM/LDAP sync; per-route RBAC available for Dedicated.
00:31:30 Elena: Our compliance team wants 7-year audit logs archived—do you support that?
00:31:36 Liam: Long-retention archives can be exported to your S3 and we support lifecycle rules. There's an add-on fee for extended retention beyond standard 13 months.
00:31:49 Samir: Final quick question—if we go Dedicated and need to pin a quantized model, can we still get Redwood Optimize recommendations?
00:31:58 Liam: Yes, Optimize runs offline evals and can recommend quantization profiles even for pinned models. The recommendations include expected cost/quality deltas.

00:31:58 Maya: Okay I'm going to call out the specific next steps:
00:32:05 Maya: 1) Redwood sends benchmark harness + test plan (Maya)
00:32:09 Maya: 2) LedgerFlow shares anonymized traces + Okta contact (Caroline/Dev)
00:32:14 Maya: 3) Redwood SE runs a profiling pass and shares results (Liam)
00:32:19 Maya: 4) Pricing and Dedicated pilot agreement (Maya)

00:32:25 Caroline: We'll aim to get traces to you by Friday.
00:32:29 Dev: We'll anonymize and drop into the secure S3 link.
00:32:33 Maya: Great. Anything else?
00:32:36 Samir: Nope. Thanks all.
00:32:39 Liam: Thanks, bye.

--- End of transcript (partial: 52m meeting, excerpts included).

Notes on transcription quality: several technical terms mis-transcribed ("KV cash" vs KV cache; some timestamps approximate).

Shared artifacts referenced during call:
- Demo harness URL: https://redwood.ai/harnesses/ledgerflow-edge-demo (internal)
- Timeout tuning doc: https://redwood.ai/docs/timeout-tuning
- Quantization impact table (internal): link in follow-up email

Potential risks noted:
- Very long context workloads increase memory pressure and cost; naive TTLs can lead to rewarm costs.
- Streaming timeouts at the gateway require client-side resume logic to avoid poor UX.
